*Corol.* Hence, from the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* of the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be gathered most approximately.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and thus the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent <note>indicator of a physical quantity</note> of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance to gravity will be as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum; entirely as demonstrated in prop. xxviii.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipse most approximately. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity at any given place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* applied to the diameter *AB* of a circle. Accordingly, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities in the individual points of *Ba* itself are most approximately to the velocities in the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate applied to the circle or ellipse described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipse most approximately. Since the resistance is assumed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the middle point *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, with center *O* and semiaxes *OB* and *OV*, will most approximately equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it. Therefore, *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of the radius, or approximately as 11 to 7: And therefore, $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the squared ratio of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be nearly a parabola having the vertex *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore will be approximately equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*. Therefore, the rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and therefore *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and for this reason, the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton provides a geometric proof for calculating the loss of motion in a pendulum caused by air resistance, comparing it to gravity under different resistance models such as linear and squared velocity.</summary>

A black stone, similar to a bean, is found in the Nile; when this is seen, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog’s tongue placed under the thumb in your shoe, or if you carry the dried heart of a dog with you, according to Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic philosopher</note>; or hare’s fur or dung, according to Pliny. Or you shall carry the tail of a young weasel cut off in your foot <note>likely meaning in one's shoe or sandal</note>, or give it a frog in a morsel of food; all these are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman philosopher and polymath</note> says that dogs flee the sight of anyone all day who expels a tick from a dog and carries it for a while. Oppian <note>A Greek author of didactic poetry on hunting and fishing</note>:

> But if you carry a small piece cut from a hyena’s skin,
> Immediately the puppies and the fierce dogs,
> Astonished by sharp terror, will not bark at you
> As you approach, even if they were barking before.

### *That a dog may not be able to run.*

If you smear the wings with oil, for it will be hindered in running; in this way, it will happen.

### *That a hawk may be spirited.*

You shall animate the bird against its prey, so that it attacks large birds; moisten the bait, which it uses at the time of hunting, with wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you want it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from its beak into a pigeon chick, then make it fly. Thus:

### *You will make partridges more combative,*

If you give them twigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more combative,*

By giving garlic in their food when they are about to fight; from which most facetiously in ancient comedy they are called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-fed</gloss>, that is, garlic-stuffed, used for someone vehement and overly prone to fighting.

### *That a bird may not fly high,*

Pull out the feathers of the tail, which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *That a bird may not be able to fly,*

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way, they do not escape in aviaries.

Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. 

Thus the sun, just like the world, is everlasting; so too is he forever the governor of living things, or rather the provider and dispenser of their total vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living beings, or the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He dispensed life to all vital beings once and for all by an eternal law, according to this manner which I shall describe.

# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first is clear. There is no doubt that just as men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or others. But in that case, the demons are not operating through the witches of whom mention is made here. And by this, the solution to the second also becomes clear. But as to the point that because God more broadly permits the generative power to be bewitched, etc., therefore it is also permitted that that member be truly and really removed, this argument does not hold, because this would not occur by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such acts, as they do not have the power to restore the member whenever they wish and know. From this it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>the art of illusion/sleight of hand</gloss>. 

Regarding the third, concerning the transformation of Lot’s wife, we say that it was real and not by the art of illusion; whereas here we are speaking of the art of illusion. 

Regarding the fourth, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said regarding the magicians of Pharaoh that they created real serpents, and demons can produce certain effects regarding some imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding humans, for whom God has greater care, according to that passage: "Does God care for oxen?" Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always, with God's permission, harm humans truly and really, or also by the art of illusion; and through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

# Question X. Whether witches operate upon humans by transforming them into beastly forms through the art of illusion.

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where they also transform humans into beasts. Regarding how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. <note>original: "xxvi. q. v. Epi. ex cōsilio acquirensi." — this refers to the Decretals of Gratian, Part 2, Causa 26, Question 5, Chapter 12, citing the Council of Ancyra</note> Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or into another appearance, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan. And let us use the arguments of <term>Saint Thomas</term> <gloss>Aquinas</gloss> in his <term>Second Book of Sentences</term>, distinction 8: whether demons can imprint illusions upon the bodily senses. Where, firstly, he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere, but it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species except that which is received from things, and there is no real beast there according to the cited canonical authority. Nor again can it be in the thing that is seen, such as when a woman appears to be a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at the same time and at once. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot be anywhere, no deceptive illusion can occur in the eye of the viewer, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. 

Furthermore, if it is said that this form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be; firstly, because air is not receptive to any form or figure; and secondly, because the same air cannot remain around that person due to its fluidity, particularly when it moves. Thirdly, because such a transformation would be seen by everyone, which does not happen, since demons are not seen to deceive the visions of holy men at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But everything passive is moved by an active agent proportioned to it. Now, the active agent proportioned to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if referring, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor even the medium as if conveying it. Regarding the first, namely that it cannot be the object, it is because it cannot be derived from any thing, as touched upon in the previous argument, since it does not occur in the sense from a thing received, nor in the thing itself, nor even in the air itself as if in a referring medium, as was touched upon previously in the third argument. For Plato believes that vision is formed according to clarity, namely that which flows from the eyes to the external air as one, and that which is brought back from light originating from bodies to meet it. Furthermore, he posits that the vision which exists in the intermediate air is easily diffused and turns, being coextensive with the fire-like faculty of sight. Galen agrees with Plato, but Hipparchus says that rays are extended from the eyes to the bodies, touching them as if with a certain palpitation, and that this renders them perceptible to the sight. The Epicureans, however, affirm that the images of things that appear insert themselves into the eyes. Aristotle believes that the images are not themselves bodies, but that they arrive from visible objects to the sight through an alteration of the air which surrounds them. Porphyry, however, considers neither rays nor images, nor anything else, to be the cause of seeing; rather, it is the soul itself, knowing itself to be visible, and being one for all, knowing itself in all things that exist. But the geometers and opticians, leaning somewhat toward Hipparchus, subscribe to certain cones formed from the coincidence of rays, which are emitted through the eyes. From this, they believe that sight comprehends many visible things at once, but those things most accurately where the rays coincide. But indeed, Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alchindus"; the Latinized name of the 9th-century philosopher Al-Kindi</note> teaches something else entirely regarding aspects. Now, someone properly exalts oneself when they say something about themselves that is above themselves. This occurs in two ways: sometimes someone speaks of themselves not indeed above that which is in them, but above that which men opine of them; which the Apostle, avoiding, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth in me, or heareth anything of me.* — In another way, someone exalts oneself by words, speaking of oneself above that which is in oneself according to the truth of the matter. And because one is more to be judged according to what is in oneself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is that it is more properly called boasting when someone exalts oneself above what is in oneself than when one exalts oneself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting, strictly speaking, is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds concerning boasting as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way, according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body [of the article], and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way, according to its cause, from which, although not always, yet more frequently it happens, and thus it indeed proceeds from pride as from an interior motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is elevated interiorly through arrogance above themselves, it follows for the most part that they outwardly boast of certain greater things about themselves, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and takes pleasure in this, because such is their habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is exalted above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is, for the most part, its cause. And for this reason, Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. ### PROCESS LXXVII.
**Tincture of Tartarized Tartar.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Tartarized Tartar, duly prepared according to Process 75, and dried, then ground into a fine powder. Pour over it, in a tall chemical vial, the purest Alcohol of wine to a depth of four inches. Then, with the vial closed only with paper, let them boil together, as gently as possible, in our wooden furnace for the space of twenty-four hours. The Alcohol will be of a golden color, floating on top, with an aromatic odor and a penetrating, warm taste. If this is repeated with fresh Alcohol in the same manner, a white salt will eventually be left at the bottom. The tinctures are thickened by a gentle fire, so that a tenth part remains, concentrated at the bottom.

#### USES.
**I**t serves to demonstrate the part in that Salt which is dissolved by the Alcohol. The Tincture itself, when prepared, is aromatic and warming, and consolidates ulcers and wounds. The remaining salt, being simpler than before, teaches that salts themselves can be whitened, once the tincture has been drawn out by the aid of Alcohol.

### PROCESS LXXVIII.
**Dissolution of Regenerated Tartar in Alcohol.**

#### APPARATUS.
**T**ake Regenerated Tartar, prepared as neatly as possible beforehand, and, as safely as can be done, pour six times its amount of the purest Alcohol into a tall, glass chemical vial. Boil it over a gentle fire in our wooden furnace, as prudently as possible. They will combine with each other, and these will become one uniformly composed substance, with the dregs deposited at the bottom. After they have then settled accurately through rest, let the supernatant and pure liquor flow off by a careful tilting of the vessel. If any saline matter not yet dissolved remains, it can be dissolved by the application of fresh Alcohol with the same caution, and separated from the dregs. Then indeed, let the prepared liquors be thickened by distilling over a very gentle fire until they are reduced to half, and the Tincture of this Salt will be obtained.

#### USES.
**Y**ou see in this experiment united into one: alkali, oily acid, and the oil of spirits of vegetables. Hence, the most active principles of plants are freed from inert earth; yet at the same time they are sufficiently safe, and their acrimony is no longer dangerous. These, indeed, when thus united, seem to constitute even the small Elixir of the Sages, which the masters of the ancient Art recommended for preserving and restoring health. It heals almost all obstructions, penetrates through the vessels, <column-break/>
and excites life with an agreeable stimulus: it heals through perspiration. In chemical operations, it also provides a most effective solvent, by which substances are reduced to their smallest parts, with their active, seminal virtue unimpaired, so that they may be admitted into the inner chambers of the body to check and tame whatever is rebellious. Nor is this remedy less praised for the beauty of the effects it produces on external bodily ailments, wounds, ulcers, and tumors. Yet this remedy, being so wholesome, should not be denied to the poor out of ambition: for it can be prepared immediately by mixing potash <note>original: "Cineres clavellatos"</note> with fifteen parts of the sharpest Vinegar, filtering, and thickening it. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, since the weakness of the Law was such that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to explain what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not make its worshippers perfect according to conscience, and that through the victims of beasts, it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness. He concludes, therefore, that it was a shadow in the very thing of future goods, not a living image of the things, and that therefore it had no other duty than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, there would be a great disagreement between the two Testaments, but since the status of the question leads us elsewhere, we must tend toward finding the truth. Let us, therefore, place in the middle the covenant which God ratified once and for all as eternal and never to perish. The completion of that covenant, from which it finally derives its status as ratified and firm, is Christ. This came into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. Although these were merely accidents of the covenant, or certainly accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories, yet because they were instruments of administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as it is accustomed to be given to other Sacraments. 3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to belong to that light, still exist, for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form through light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which make up so much of the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has perception only of such things as are of the light of the world, and not of such as are of the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the universal heaven is in that light. This light, namely the light of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. The things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world, which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for life from that source is within the things that are of the light of the world. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? All are forced to admit this. If this, therefore, is true, I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and the useful? And the good taken, and the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it must be so, I ask you to explain to me: how is it separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But in order to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted of admitting that poison lies there, and you are asked where at last that poison goes: then I do not know what you bring forth regarding "corrections," which allegedly extract and remove the poison,

just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or later with <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>a preparation of scammony</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards as it was at first? And yet, in the meantime, you boast that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone?
<margin>Diagridium.</margin>
It remains in the <term>Diagridium</term>. Test this, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know that not sluggishly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, and call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be administered to horses. Make an experiment by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose: you will see if you are not going to feel the poison.
<margin>What a Physician's correction is.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections, too; it is situated with them, not with you. Now, in this case, there is nothing for a Physician to consider further than that the poison be removed. That must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without any harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely, that there is a need for a similar separation. That not yet done, you cannot be secure in your operation: unless perhaps it happens that nature supplies your turns, or the greater beneficence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, there will be no help remaining.

Therefore, since the true foundation—if it is to be called such—is that which removes the poison, [consider] how Alchemy performs this. For this must be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed, and if Saturn is situated in Venus, it is separated from it. For as many as are the ascendants and impressions in the things of nature, just so many bodies exist in them. But as for those bodies which are contrary, it is necessary that some part of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil which you seek may be removed from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useless for anything, unless it is first cast into the fire: so much less useful is medicine that does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduct and assist man. And should this not deservedly be considered the approved foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret remedies</gloss>.
